note: THE CONTENT DOCUMENT — the course. This is the slot the course goes in: one document, loaded through src/lib/contentLoader.js and checked by src/lib/contentSchema.js, so adding the course is a data change here rather than a code change anywhere. The general-knowledge set that used to sit here came out for the beta (`git log -- src/content/test-content.json` is where it lives if it is ever wanted back); from 2026-09-21 it holds the owner's own material, starting with Module 13d's first chapter, and the `content.test` switch in src/lib/flags.js is on for everyone so every visitor loads it. Module NAMES are here and in src/data.js, and the two must agree: data.js is what the Flight Deck draws before this document arrives. Module CODES (M1–M4) never change — progress and saves are keyed to them.
contentModel: modules[] -> chapters[] -> lessons[] and one quiz per chapter. A chapter may also carry cards[] — its study-card set, same shape as a quiz question; without it the card set is the quiz's questions. A module may carry downloads[] — {id, title, file, pages}, a file under public/ offered as a plain download, never opened in the reader. notes, threads, replies, people and presence are the lesson surface's own rows. See contentSchema.js for the exact shape and the validator that enforces it.

questions.question: What is the chord of a rotor blade
options: A straight line from the blade root to the blade tip
A curved line along the upper surface of the blade
A straight line from the leading edge to the trailing edge
questions.explain: The chord is the straight reference line from leading edge to trailing edge.

questions.question: How is the relative wind directed in relation to the flight path of the blade
options: Always along the same flight path
Always perpendicular to the path
Always opposite to the flight path
questions.explain: The relative wind is always opposite to the blade's flight path.

questions.question: What is the pitch angle
options: The acute angle between the chord and the plane of rotation
The acute angle between the chord and the relative wind
The acute angle between the axis and the plane of rotation
questions.explain: Pitch angle is measured from the plane of rotation to the chord.

questions.question: What is the angle of attack
options: The acute angle between the chord line and the relative wind
The acute angle between the relative wind and the plane of rotation
The acute angle between the chord line and the plane of rotation
questions.explain: Angle of attack is chord line to relative wind.

questions.question: When is the angle of attack equal to the pitch angle
options: When the relative wind is perpendicular to the plane of rotation
When the relative wind is parallel to the axis of rotation
When the relative wind is in the same direction as the plane of rotation
questions.explain: If the relative wind lies in the plane of rotation, both angles use the same reference line.

questions.question: The pilot holds the pitch angle constant, but outside influences change the relative wind. What happens to the angle of attack?
options: It becomes equal to the pitch angle of the blade
It changes, because it depends on the relative wind
It stays constant, because the pitch is constant
questions.explain: Angle of attack is also affected by relative wind changes, not only by pitch.

questions.question: In which direction does lift act in relation to the relative wind
options: Perpendicular to the relative wind
Opposite to the relative wind
Parallel to the relative wind
questions.explain: Lift is perpendicular to the relative wind.

questions.question: Where does the output occur when a force is applied to a turning rotor
options: 180° later in the direction of rotation
90° earlier in the direction of rotation
90° later in the direction of rotation
questions.explain: The output appears 90° later in the direction of rotation.

questions.question: Why must the steering input to the rotor be applied 90° before the point where the tilt is wanted
options: Because the swash plate is mounted 90° to the rotor
Because the output occurs 90° later in the direction of rotation
Because the output occurs 90° earlier in the direction of rotation
questions.explain: Precession shifts the result 90° in the direction of rotation, so the input must lead by 90°.

questions.question: A helicopter rotor turns counterclockwise. The tip-path plane must tilt backward for rearward flight. Following the precession rule, where must the downward force be put in?
options: On the left side
Right at the rear
On the right side
questions.explain: The output is wanted at the rear; 90° earlier in counterclockwise rotation is the left side.

questions.question: Which law explains torque reaction on a helicopter fuselage
options: Newton's Second Law
Newton's law of inertia
Newton's Third Law
questions.explain: Torque reaction is action and reaction, Newton's Third Law.

questions.question: In a helicopter with a main rotor and a tail rotor, which component compensates the torque
options: The main rotor
The tail rotor
The swash plate
questions.explain: The tail rotor compensates torque.

questions.question: In which direction does rotor thrust always act
options: Parallel to the rotor plane
Perpendicular to the rotor plane
Along the direction of flight
questions.explain: Rotor thrust is perpendicular to the rotor plane.

questions.question: Why must the rotor plane be tilted when changing from hover to forward flight
options: Because the tail rotor thrust acts in the direction of flight
Because the rotor RPM must be increased for forward flight
Because rotor thrust always acts perpendicular to the rotor plane
questions.explain: To point thrust forward, the plane must tilt, because thrust is perpendicular to it.

questions.question: What does the pilot do to the main rotor blades by moving the collective lever upwards
options: Increases the pitch angle of each blade once per revolution
Tilts the rotor plane in the direction of flight
Increases the pitch angle of all blades at the same time
questions.explain: Collective up raises the pitch of all blades together.

questions.question: Besides changing the blade pitch, which other effect does a movement of the collective lever have?
options: It changes engine power and causes effects like torque
It tilts the rotor plane and causes translating tendency
It changes tail rotor pitch and causes precession
questions.explain: Collective movement also changes engine power and torque effects.

questions.question: What do the pedals change
options: The pitch angle of the main rotor blades
The pitch angle of the tail rotor blades
The tilt of the main rotor plane
questions.explain: Pedals change tail rotor blade pitch.

questions.question: How is the collective pitch change achieved at the swash plate
options: By rotating the stationary swash plate
By lifting or lowering the swash plate
By tilting the swash plate to one side
questions.explain: Collective raises or lowers the swash plate.

questions.question: How is the cyclic pitch change achieved at the swash plate
options: By lifting the whole swash plate
By tilting the swash plate
By turning the stationary part
questions.explain: Cyclic tilts the swash plate.

questions.question: During a control check the swash plate tilts but its mean height does not change. Which pitch change is being made?
options: Cyclic pitch change
Tail rotor pitch change
Collective pitch change
questions.explain: Tilting the swash plate produces cyclic pitch change.

questions.question: Why does the swash plate have to act as an interface
options: It transfers engine power between the main gearbox and the rotating rotor mast
It transfers torque between the main rotor and the tail rotor drive system
It transfers control signals between the stationary input system and the rotating rotor
questions.explain: Cockpit inputs are stationary but the blades rotate, so the swash plate links the two.

questions.question: Which statement correctly assigns the swash plate parts?
options: Upper part rotating, lower part stationary
Both parts rotating with the rotor
Upper part stationary, lower part rotating
questions.explain: The upper part rotates; the lower part is stationary.

questions.question: What is dissymmetry of lift
options: The difference in lift between main and tail rotor
The difference in lift between advancing and retreating blade
The difference in lift in and out of ground effect
questions.explain: The lift difference between advancing and retreating blade is dissymmetry of lift.

questions.question: Why does the advancing blade produce more lift in forward flight
options: The opposing airstream is added to its rotational speed
Its pitch angle is increased by the collective
The opposing airstream is subtracted from its rotational speed
questions.explain: The airstream adds to its speed, giving more lift.

questions.question: Why is the installation of a lead-lag hinge required
options: Flapping blades change the direction of the torque reaction
Flapping blades change their pitch angle during each revolution
Flapping blades accelerate or decelerate and move forward or backward
questions.explain: The forward and backward blade movement caused by flapping must be allowed by a lead-lag hinge.

questions.question: In forward flight the advancing blade flaps up. Combining the flapping and centre-of-mass facts, how does this blade move in the plane of rotation?
options: It accelerates and moves forward (leads)
It decelerates and moves backward (lags)
It keeps its position in the plane
questions.explain: The advancing blade flaps up, its CG moves inward, so it accelerates and moves forward.

questions.question: Why does the advancing blade flap up
options: It experiences decreased relative wind and generates less lift
It experiences increased relative wind and generates more lift
Its centre of gravity moves closer to the blade tip
questions.explain: More relative wind means more lift, so it flaps up.

questions.question: Is blade flapping alone sufficient to restore rotor balance
options: No, it helps to balance but is not sufficient
No, it increases the dissymmetry of lift
Yes, it fully restores rotor balance
questions.explain: Flapping helps but does not fully restore balance.

questions.question: When are lead-lag movements always generated
options: When the rotor RPM is held constant
When a rotor blade is flapping
When the rotor hovers in ground effect
questions.explain: Flapping always generates lead-lag movement.

questions.question: What is translating tendency
options: The drift caused by the ground effect air cushion
The turning of the fuselage opposite to the rotor
The drift caused by the thrust of the tail rotor
questions.explain: Translating tendency is the tail-rotor-thrust drift.

questions.question: How may the pilot prevent the lateral drift due to translating tendency
options: Tilt the main rotor disk slightly opposite to the drift
Tilt the main rotor disk slightly in the drift direction
Reduce the tail rotor thrust until the drift stops
questions.explain: The disk is tilted slightly opposite to the drift.

questions.question: During hover, tail rotor thrust makes the helicopter drift to the right. How must the main rotor disk be tilted to prevent this?
options: Slightly forward
Slightly to the right
Slightly to the left
questions.explain: The disk is tilted opposite to the drift, so to the left for a right drift.

questions.question: Within which height is a helicopter operating in ground effect
options: Within one rotor diameter
Within two rotor diameters
Within half a rotor diameter
questions.explain: In-ground effect is within one rotor diameter.

questions.question: How does the power required to hover in ground effect compare with hovering out of ground effect?
options: The same power is required in both
Less power is required in ground effect
More power is required in ground effect
questions.explain: Hovering in ground effect needs less power.

questions.question: A helicopter hovering out of ground effect descends into an in-ground effect hover. What happens to blade efficiency and why?
options: It increases, because the reduced downward airflow increases the angle of attack
It decreases, because the increased downward airflow reduces the angle of attack
It increases, because the pilot must increase the pitch angle of the blades
questions.explain: Reduced downwash raises angle of attack and efficiency.

questions.question: A pilot descends from an out-of-ground effect hover into ground effect and wants to remain in the ground effect hover. What must he do and why?
options: Keep the blade pitch angle, because efficiency is unchanged
Increase the blade pitch angle, because rotor efficiency decreases
Reduce the blade pitch angle, because rotor efficiency increases
questions.explain: Entering ground effect raises angle of attack and efficiency, so pitch is reduced to stay in the hover.

questions.question: Why must the rotor RPM be sustained after an engine failure
options: So that the tail rotor can be stopped during the descent
So that the engine can be restarted during the descent
So that a controlled flight can be continued to the ground
questions.explain: Rotor RPM keeps the helicopter controllable to the ground.

questions.question: How is the rotor driving force controlled in autorotation
options: By adjusting the tail rotor pedals
By adjusting the collective pitch
By adjusting the engine power lever
questions.explain: The collective pitch controls it.

questions.question: An engine fails in cruise. In which order does the pilot use energy during the autorotation?
options: Rotor kinetic energy cushions the descent, then altitude drives the rotor at touchdown
Altitude drives the rotor in the descent, then rotor kinetic energy cushions touchdown
Engine power drives the rotor in the descent, then altitude cushions touchdown
questions.explain: Phase 1 converts altitude into rotor energy; phase 2 uses the rotor energy for touchdown.

questions.question: In which direction does the airflow pass through the main rotor during an autorotative descent
options: From bottom to top
From top to bottom
From front to rear
questions.explain: In autorotation air flows up through the rotor.

cards.question: What is the primary airfoil of the helicopter
options: The main rotor
The fuselage
The tail rotor
cards.explain: The manual names the main rotor as the helicopter's primary airfoil.

cards.question: Why is the helicopter often referred to as a rotary-wing aircraft
options: Its fuselage acts as a rotating wing
Its primary airfoil is the tail rotor
Its primary airfoil is the main rotor
cards.explain: Because its main lifting surface is a rotating rotor, the helicopter is called rotary-wing.

cards.question: What is an airfoil by definition
options: Any surface which generates a useful static pressure of the air
Only a wing surface which generates lift in forward flight
Any surface which generates a useful dynamic reaction of the air
cards.explain: The manual defines an airfoil as any surface giving a useful dynamic reaction of the air.

cards.question: Which two forces are named as the useful reaction of the air on an airfoil
options: Lift and thrust
Thrust and weight
Lift and drag
cards.explain: The text names lift and thrust as the two forces needed for flying and manoeuvring.

cards.question: What are the airfoils of the main rotor
options: The swash plate
The rotor blades
The rotor mast
cards.explain: The blades are the main rotor airfoils.

cards.question: What is the root of a rotor blade
options: The outer end of the blade opposite the rotor mast
The end where the blade is attached to the rotor mast
The distance from the blade attachment to the outer end
cards.explain: The root is the blade end attached to the rotor mast.

cards.question: What is the tip of a rotor blade
options: The inner end of the blade, at the rotor mast
The outer end of the blade, opposite the root
The front edge that cuts into the wind
cards.explain: The tip is the outer end, opposite the root.

cards.question: What is the span of a rotor blade
options: The distance from leading edge to trailing edge
The distance from one blade tip to the opposite blade tip
The distance from root to tip along the blade centerline
cards.explain: Span is measured root to tip along the centerline.

cards.question: A technician measures a rotor blade from the attachment point at the rotor mast to its outer end, along its centerline. Which dimension is being measured?
options: The span
The chord
The pitch
cards.explain: Root to tip along the centerline is the span; the chord runs leading edge to trailing edge.

cards.question: What is the leading edge of a rotor blade
options: The edge that cuts into the wind when the rotor is turning
The outer end of the blade opposite the root
The edge opposite the one that cuts into the wind
cards.explain: The leading edge cuts into the wind.

cards.question: What is the trailing edge of a rotor blade
options: The edge opposite the leading edge
The end attached to the rotor mast
The edge that cuts into the wind
cards.explain: The trailing edge is opposite the leading edge.

cards.question: What is the chord of a rotor blade
options: A curved line along the upper surface of the blade
A straight line from the blade root to the blade tip
A straight line from the leading edge to the trailing edge
cards.explain: The chord is the straight reference line from leading edge to trailing edge.

cards.question: Looking at the cross section of a rotor blade, a straight reference line is drawn from the front edge to the rear edge. What is this line called?
options: The pitch
The chord
The span
cards.explain: That reference line in the cross section is the chord.

cards.question: What is the advancing blade
options: The backward moving blade
The blade at the tail boom
The forward moving blade
cards.explain: The blade moving forward is the advancing blade.

cards.question: What is the retreating blade
options: The blade over the cockpit
The backward moving blade
The forward moving blade
cards.explain: The blade moving backward is the retreating blade.

cards.question: What is the relative wind
options: The direction of the airflow with respect to the rotor blade
The direction of the airflow with respect to the ground
The speed of the natural wind at the landing site
cards.explain: Relative wind is airflow direction relative to the blade.

cards.question: How is the relative wind directed in relation to the flight path of the blade
options: Always perpendicular to the path
Always opposite to the flight path
Always along the same flight path
cards.explain: The relative wind is always opposite to the blade's flight path.

cards.question: A blade moves horizontally forward. In which direction does the relative wind move
options: Horizontally backward
Backward and upward
Horizontally forward
cards.explain: The relative wind is exactly opposite: horizontally backward.

cards.question: A blade moves forward and downward. In which direction does the relative wind move
options: Backward and upward
Forward and upward
Backward and downward
cards.explain: Exactly opposite to forward-and-downward is backward-and-upward.

cards.question: On the retreating side a blade moves horizontally backward. Which relative wind acts on it
options: Vertically upward
Horizontally forward
Horizontally backward
cards.explain: Relative wind is always exactly opposite to blade movement.

cards.question: A blade is moving forward and at the same time flapping upward. Applying the rule for relative wind, from which direction does the relative wind come?
options: Backward and downward
Backward and upward
Forward and downward
cards.explain: The relative wind moves exactly opposite to the blade path, so forward-and-upward blade motion gives a backward-and-downward relative wind.

cards.question: Which two movements of the rotor blades are given as factors affecting the relative wind
options: Turning and flapping
Turning and folding
Leading and feathering
cards.explain: The manual names turning and flapping of the blades.

cards.question: A helicopter stands with its rotor stopped while wind blows over the blades. Which statement about the relative wind is correct?
options: There is no relative wind because the rotor is stopped
The relative wind is created only by blade flapping
The wind blowing over the blade creates the relative wind
cards.explain: Even with the rotor stopped, wind over the blade is airflow relative to the blade.

cards.question: What is the axis of rotation
options: The plane formed by the average tip path
The axis around which the rotor blades are turning
The line from the leading edge to the trailing edge
cards.explain: The rotor blades turn around the axis of rotation.

cards.question: What forms the plane of rotation
options: The average tip path of the blades
The flapping hinges of the blades
The chord line of the blades
cards.explain: The plane of rotation is formed by the average blade tip path.

cards.question: How is the plane of rotation arranged with respect to the axis of rotation
options: At the pitch angle to it
Parallel to it
Perpendicular to it
cards.explain: The plane of rotation is perpendicular to the axis.

cards.question: A helicopter is flying and the blades flap during each revolution, so each tip follows a slightly different path. Which path defines the plane of rotation?
options: The path of the blade roots
The average tip path of the blades
The highest tip path of the blades
cards.explain: The manual defines it by the average tip path.

cards.question: What is the pitch angle
options: The acute angle between the chord and the plane of rotation
The acute angle between the chord and the relative wind
The acute angle between the axis and the plane of rotation
cards.explain: Pitch angle is measured from the plane of rotation to the chord.

cards.question: Which cockpit control changes the pitch angle of all main rotor blades
options: The tail rotor pedals
The collective pitch control
The cyclic pitch stick
cards.explain: The collective pitch control changes the pitch angle.

cards.question: Around which axis does the blade rotate when the pitch angle is changed with the collective pitch control
options: The flapping hinge axis
The hub axis
The helicopter lateral axis
cards.explain: The manual says the blade rotates around the hub axis.

cards.question: Which term is often confused with the pitch angle
options: The flapping angle
The angle of attack
The angle of rotation
cards.explain: The note warns that pitch angle is often confused with angle of attack.

cards.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes pitch angle from angle of attack?
options: Pitch angle is referenced to the plane of rotation, angle of attack to the relative wind
Pitch angle is referenced to the relative wind, angle of attack to the plane of rotation
Pitch angle is referenced to the axis of rotation, angle of attack to the span line
cards.explain: Both use the chord, but pitch angle uses the plane of rotation and angle of attack uses the relative wind.

cards.question: What is the angle of attack
options: The acute angle between the chord line and the relative wind
The acute angle between the relative wind and the plane of rotation
The acute angle between the chord line and the plane of rotation
cards.explain: Angle of attack is chord line to relative wind.

cards.question: Besides the pitch angle, what can the pilot also vary by operating the collective pitch control?
options: The plane of rotation
The blade span
The angle of attack
cards.explain: The angle of attack can also be varied with the collective.

cards.question: Why do the same factors that affect the relative wind also affect the angle of attack
options: Because the relative wind depends upon the pitch angle
Because the angle of attack depends upon the blade span
Because the angle of attack depends upon the relative wind
cards.explain: Angle of attack is measured to the relative wind, so what changes one changes the other.

cards.question: When is the angle of attack equal to the pitch angle
options: When the relative wind is parallel to the axis of rotation
When the relative wind is perpendicular to the plane of rotation
When the relative wind is in the same direction as the plane of rotation
cards.explain: If the relative wind lies in the plane of rotation, both angles use the same reference line.

cards.question: The pilot increases the pitch angle. What happens to the angle of attack
options: It remains unchanged
It is also increased
It is decreased
cards.explain: Pitch and angle of attack change together.

cards.question: The pilot lowers the collective and so reduces the pitch angle. What happens to the angle of attack?
options: It remains unchanged
It is increased
It is also decreased
cards.explain: Decreasing pitch also decreases the angle of attack.

cards.question: The pilot holds the pitch angle constant, but outside influences change the relative wind. What happens to the angle of attack?
options: It changes, because it depends on the relative wind
It stays constant, because the pitch is constant
It becomes equal to the pitch angle of the blade
cards.explain: Angle of attack is also affected by relative wind changes, not only by pitch.

cards.question: How can the pilot increase or decrease the angle of attack
options: By moving the pitch angle of the rotor blade
By moving the plane of rotation of the rotor
By changing the span of the rotor blade
cards.explain: The pilot changes the angle of attack through the blade pitch angle.

cards.question: In the figure 'Angle of Attack', the relative wind comes from slightly below the plane of rotation. How does the angle of attack compare with the pitch angle?
options: The angle of attack is smaller than the pitch angle
The angle of attack is larger than the pitch angle
The angle of attack equals the pitch angle
cards.explain: The figure shows the angle of attack as the larger angle because the relative wind is inclined below the plane of rotation.

cards.question: What is lift
options: The force produced by torque reaction
The force that is produced by gravity
The force that is produced by the airfoil
cards.explain: Lift is the airfoil's force.

cards.question: In which direction does lift act in relation to the relative wind
options: Opposite to the relative wind
Perpendicular to the relative wind
Parallel to the relative wind
cards.explain: Lift is perpendicular to the relative wind.

cards.question: What is lift required to counteract
options: Drag
Gravity
Torque
cards.explain: Lift counteracts gravity.

cards.question: To which bodies does gyroscopic precession apply
options: All rotating bodies
Only the main rotor
Only the tail rotor
cards.explain: It applies to all rotating bodies, including both rotors.

cards.question: How is gyroscopic precession defined
options: The change of the rotational axis as a result of an external force
The turning of the fuselage opposite to the rotor
The change of the rotor RPM as a result of an external force
cards.explain: Precession is a change of the rotational axis caused by an external force.

cards.question: Where does the output occur when a force is applied to a turning rotor
options: 90° earlier in the direction of rotation
180° later in the direction of rotation
90° later in the direction of rotation
cards.explain: The output appears 90° later in the direction of rotation.

cards.question: From which point is the 90° of gyroscopic precession measured
options: From the point of the input
From the blade root
From the nose of the helicopter
cards.explain: The 90° is measured from the point of input.

cards.question: In the example wheel, an external force tries to turn the wheel around the input axis. Around which axis does the movement actually take place?
options: Only around the spin axis
Only around the input axis
Around the output axis
cards.explain: Because of precession the movement occurs around the output axis.

cards.question: For a helicopter whose rotor turns counterclockwise, where must the downward force be put in to tilt the tip-path plane forward?
options: Right in front
On the left side
On the right side
cards.explain: The manual states the input goes exactly on the right side.

cards.question: In which direction must the tip-path plane be tilted for the helicopter to fly forward
options: To the right
Backward
Forward
cards.explain: Forward flight needs a forward-tilted tip-path plane.

cards.question: Why must the steering input to the rotor be applied 90° before the point where the tilt is wanted
options: Because the output occurs 90° later in the direction of rotation
Because the swash plate is mounted 90° to the rotor
Because the output occurs 90° earlier in the direction of rotation
cards.explain: Precession shifts the result 90° in the direction of rotation, so the input must lead by 90°.

cards.question: A downward force is applied on the right side of a counterclockwise turning rotor. Where does the output appear?
options: Right at the rear
On the left side
Right in front
cards.explain: 90° later in counterclockwise rotation from the right side is the front.

cards.question: A helicopter rotor turns counterclockwise. The tip-path plane must tilt backward for rearward flight. Following the precession rule, where must the downward force be put in?
options: On the left side
Right at the rear
On the right side
cards.explain: The output is wanted at the rear; 90° earlier in counterclockwise rotation is the left side.

cards.question: A helicopter rotor turns counterclockwise. The tip-path plane must tilt to the left. Following the precession rule, where must the downward force be put in?
options: Right at the rear
On the left side
Right in front
cards.explain: The output is wanted on the left; 90° earlier in counterclockwise rotation is the front.

cards.question: A downward force is applied at the rear of a counterclockwise turning rotor. Where does the tip-path plane tilt down?
options: On the left side
On the right side
Right in front
cards.explain: 90° later than the rear in counterclockwise rotation is the right side.

cards.question: Which law explains torque reaction on a helicopter fuselage
options: Newton's Second Law
Newton's Third Law
Newton's law of inertia
cards.explain: Torque reaction is action and reaction, Newton's Third Law.

cards.question: In which direction does the helicopter fuselage tend to rotate due to torque
options: Around its lateral axis, nose down
In the same direction as the rotor blades
Opposite to the direction of the rotor blades
cards.explain: Action and reaction: the fuselage turns opposite to the rotor.

cards.question: What is the effect called when the fuselage tends to rotate opposite to the rotor blades
options: Precession
Torque
Translating tendency
cards.explain: The manual calls this effect torque.

cards.question: In a helicopter with a main rotor and a tail rotor, which component compensates the torque
options: The swash plate
The tail rotor
The main rotor
cards.explain: The tail rotor compensates torque.

cards.question: In the most common helicopter design, what does the main rotor create
options: Lift and thrust
Lift and anti-torque
Thrust and anti-torque
cards.explain: The main rotor creates lift and thrust.

cards.question: A helicopter's main rotor turns counterclockwise seen from above and the tail rotor is not yet producing thrust. Which way does the fuselage tend to turn?
options: Not at all
Clockwise
Counterclockwise
cards.explain: The fuselage reaction is opposite to a counterclockwise rotor, so clockwise.

cards.question: Why does a helicopter need no pull or push propellers
options: Because the rotors are driven by the airflow
Because the rotors generate both lift and thrust
Because the tail rotor generates the thrust
cards.explain: The rotor provides both lift and thrust.

cards.question: How do the rotors of a helicopter additionally ensure directional control
options: Control surfaces on the rotor blades are deflected
The rotor RPM is changed so thrust acts in all directions
The rotor plane may be tilted so thrust can act in all directions
cards.explain: Tilting the rotor plane lets thrust act in any direction.

cards.question: What does lift counteract according to the helicopter description
options: Thrust
Torque
Weight
cards.explain: Lift counteracts weight.

cards.question: What generates the total rotor thrust
options: The advancing blade alone
All rotor blades together
The tail rotor blades
cards.explain: The note says all blades together generate total rotor thrust.

cards.question: After an engine failure or broken drive shafts, how can a helicopter land safely
options: By using translating tendency
By performing an autorotation
By using ground effect
cards.explain: Autorotation allows a safe landing without engine power.

cards.question: During an autorotation after an engine failure, which statement about control is correct?
options: Only the pedals remain effective and the touchdown point cannot be chosen
The helicopter is fully controllable and the pilot can choose the touchdown point
The helicopter is not controllable and lands wherever the descent takes it
cards.explain: The manual says it is fully controllable and the pilot selects the touchdown location.

cards.question: In the figure 'Helicopter', the total rotor thrust is split into two components. What are they called?
options: Thrust and drag
Lift and weight
Lift and thrust
cards.explain: The figure shows total rotor thrust with its lift and thrust components.

cards.question: How do helicopters change direction, unlike other aircraft
options: By changing the angle of the rotor blade plane
By changing the RPM of the main rotor
By deflecting control surfaces on the fuselage
cards.explain: Helicopters tilt the rotor blade plane instead of deflecting surfaces.

cards.question: What achieves the change of the rotor blade plane angle for directional control
options: Mechanical actuators controlled by the pilot and aerodynamic forces on the blades
Control surfaces on the fuselage and changes of the engine power by the pilot
Electric motors in the rotor head and the thrust of the tail rotor on the boom
cards.explain: The manual names pilot-controlled mechanical actuators plus aerodynamic forces.

cards.question: The pilot moves the cyclic stick forward. What does the rotor plane do
options: It tilts forward
It tilts backward
It moves upward
cards.explain: Forward cyclic tilts the rotor plane forward.

cards.question: The pilot moves the cyclic stick to the left. In which direction does the helicopter fly
options: To the right
Backward
To the left
cards.explain: Left cyclic gives flight to the left.

cards.question: In which direction does rotor thrust always act
options: Parallel to the rotor plane
Perpendicular to the rotor plane
Along the direction of flight
cards.explain: Rotor thrust is perpendicular to the rotor plane.

cards.question: Why must the rotor plane be tilted when changing from hover to forward flight
options: Because the tail rotor thrust acts in the direction of flight
Because the rotor RPM must be increased for forward flight
Because rotor thrust always acts perpendicular to the rotor plane
cards.explain: To point thrust forward, the plane must tilt, because thrust is perpendicular to it.

cards.question: What is the technical solution for tilting the rotor plane
options: Changing the rotor RPM during each revolution
Changing the blade span during each revolution
Changing the pitch angle during each revolution
cards.explain: Cyclic pitch changes during each revolution tilt the plane.

cards.question: Which movements do helicopters with one main rotor control with the principle of cyclic control?
options: Vertical and yaw movement
Longitudinal and vertical movement
Longitudinal and lateral movement
cards.explain: Cyclic control handles longitudinal and lateral movement.

cards.question: How does cyclic control create different amounts of lift within the rotor plane
options: The blade changes its angle of incidence during each revolution
All blades change their pitch angle at the same time together
The rotor RPM is increased and decreased during each revolution
cards.explain: Cyclic changes the incidence per revolution, giving different lift around the disc.

cards.question: When flying straight ahead, where does the blade reach its minimum angle of incidence
options: Right in the front
On the right side
Right at the rear
cards.explain: Minimum incidence is right in the front.

cards.question: When flying straight ahead, how many degrees after the minimum does the blade reach its maximum angle of incidence?
cards.explain: The maximum is 180° later, opposite to the direction of flight.

cards.question: In straight-ahead flight the blade has minimum incidence in front and maximum incidence at the rear. What is the result for the rotor plane?
options: It tilts backward, giving lift and rearward thrust
It stays level, giving lift but no thrust
It tilts forward, giving lift and forward thrust
cards.explain: More lift at the rear and less at the front tilts the plane forward, producing lift and forward thrust.

cards.question: The pilot moves the cyclic stick backward. In which direction does the helicopter fly
options: Backward
Upward
Forward
cards.explain: Backward cyclic tilts the plane back and the helicopter flies backward.

cards.question: What does the pilot do to the main rotor blades by moving the collective lever upwards
options: Increases the pitch angle of each blade once per revolution
Increases the pitch angle of all blades at the same time
Tilts the rotor plane in the direction of flight
cards.explain: Collective up raises the pitch of all blades together.

cards.question: The pilot moves the collective lever upwards. What does the helicopter do
options: It turns left
It descends
It climbs
cards.explain: More pitch gives more lift and the helicopter climbs.

cards.question: The pilot moves the collective lever downwards. What does the helicopter do
options: It descends
It flies backward
It climbs
cards.explain: Collective down makes the helicopter descend.

cards.question: Which hinges do the rotor blades need to change their pitch angle
options: Feathering hinges
Lead-lag hinges
Flapping hinges
cards.explain: Pitch change needs feathering hinges.

cards.question: Where are the feathering hinges mounted
options: Between the swash plate and the mast
Between the tail rotor and the gearbox
Between the rotor blade and the rotor head
cards.explain: Feathering hinges sit between blade and rotor head.

cards.question: Which parts move the rotor blades to larger pitch angles when the collective is raised
options: Drive shafts
Control rods
Flapping hinges
cards.explain: Control rods move the blades.

cards.question: Besides changing the blade pitch, which other effect does a movement of the collective lever have?
options: It tilts the rotor plane and causes translating tendency
It changes engine power and causes effects like torque
It changes tail rotor pitch and causes precession
cards.explain: Collective movement also changes engine power and torque effects.

cards.question: A pilot raises the collective lever to climb. The engine power changes and so does the torque effect on the fuselage. Which control must then vary the tail rotor thrust?
options: The collective lever
The cyclic pitch stick
The tail rotor pedals
cards.explain: Torque is compensated by the tail rotor, whose thrust the pilot varies with the pedals.

cards.question: Which control does the pilot use to turn the helicopter around the rotor mast axis
options: The cyclic pitch stick
The tail rotor pedals
The collective lever
cards.explain: Pedals turn the helicopter around the mast axis.

cards.question: What do the pedals change
options: The pitch angle of the main rotor blades
The tilt of the main rotor plane
The pitch angle of the tail rotor blades
cards.explain: Pedals change tail rotor blade pitch.

cards.question: How do the pedals vary the tail rotor thrust
options: By tilting the plane of rotation of the tail rotor
By changing the RPM of the tail rotor drive shaft
By changing the pitch angle of the tail rotor blades
cards.explain: Tail rotor thrust is varied via blade pitch.

cards.question: The pilot moves the left pedal forward. What happens to the right pedal and the helicopter
options: Right pedal moves backward; helicopter turns left
Right pedal moves backward; helicopter turns right
Right pedal moves forward; helicopter turns left
cards.explain: Left pedal forward turns the helicopter left, with the right pedal moving back.

cards.question: The pilot wants to turn the helicopter to the right around the rotor mast axis. What must he do?
options: Move the cyclic to the right
Push the left pedal forward
Push the right pedal forward
cards.explain: Right pedal forward turns the helicopter right.

cards.question: How is the collective pitch change achieved at the swash plate
options: By tilting the swash plate to one side
By lifting or lowering the swash plate
By rotating the stationary swash plate
cards.explain: Collective raises or lowers the swash plate.

cards.question: How is the cyclic pitch change achieved at the swash plate
options: By lifting the whole swash plate
By turning the stationary part
By tilting the swash plate
cards.explain: Cyclic tilts the swash plate.

cards.question: A technician watches the swash plate while a helper moves one cockpit control, and the whole swash plate moves up without tilting. Which control is being moved?
options: The cyclic stick
The collective lever
The tail pedals
cards.explain: Lifting the swash plate is collective; tilting would be cyclic.

cards.question: During a control check the swash plate tilts but its mean height does not change. Which pitch change is being made?
options: Cyclic pitch change
Tail rotor pitch change
Collective pitch change
cards.explain: Tilting the swash plate produces cyclic pitch change.

cards.question: Where is the swash plate usually located
options: Underneath the rotor plane
Above the rotor plane
Inside the tail boom
cards.explain: It is usually underneath the rotor plane.

cards.question: To which part of the swash plate are the rotor blade control rods connected
options: The lower part
The bearing
The upper part
cards.explain: Blade control rods attach to the upper part.

cards.question: Why does the swash plate have to act as an interface
options: It transfers control signals between the stationary input system and the rotating rotor
It transfers engine power between the main gearbox and the rotating rotor mast
It transfers torque between the main rotor and the tail rotor drive system
cards.explain: Cockpit inputs are stationary but the blades rotate, so the swash plate links the two.

cards.question: Which statement correctly assigns the swash plate parts?
options: Upper part rotating, lower part stationary
Both parts rotating with the rotor
Upper part stationary, lower part rotating
cards.explain: The upper part rotates; the lower part is stationary.

cards.question: How are the rotating and stationary parts of the swash plate connected
options: By a bearing
By control rods
By a flapping hinge
cards.explain: A bearing connects the two parts.

cards.question: How are the two parts of the swash plate arranged relative to each other
options: At 90° in turning direction
Perpendicular to each other
Parallel to each other
cards.explain: The two parts are parallel.

cards.question: Which parts act on the stationary part of the swash plate
options: Control rods and bell cranks connected with the cockpit controls
The main rotor blades acting through the feathering hinges
Control rods connected directly to the main rotor blades
cards.explain: The stationary part is moved by control rods and bell cranks from the cockpit.

cards.question: How is the rotating part of the swash plate connected to the main rotor blades
options: By bell cranks
By control rods
By a bearing
cards.explain: Control rods connect the rotating part to the blades.

cards.question: What is the direct result on the rotor blades when the swash plate moves?
options: The blades move forward and backward on lead-lag hinges
The control rods move and the blade pitch angle changes
The bearing locks and the blades stop their flapping
cards.explain: Swash plate motion moves control rods, which change pitch.

cards.question: Of which two parts does the swash plate consist
options: A rotating part and a stationary part
An upper rotating part and a rotating bearing
A cyclic part and a collective part
cards.explain: The swash plate has a rotating and a stationary part.

cards.question: In a hover with no wind, how does the lift of the rotor blades compare
options: All blades generate the same amount of lift
The retreating blade generates more lift
The advancing blade generates more lift
cards.explain: In a no-wind hover all blades have the same parameters.

cards.question: What is dissymmetry of lift
options: The difference in lift between advancing and retreating blade
The difference in lift in and out of ground effect
The difference in lift between main and tail rotor
cards.explain: The lift difference between advancing and retreating blade is dissymmetry of lift.

cards.question: What is the crucial factor causing dissymmetry of lift when the helicopter flies
options: The interference of the ground surface
The airstream caused by the speed of flight
The torque reaction of the main rotor
cards.explain: The flight airstream adds to or subtracts from blade speed.

cards.question: Why does the advancing blade produce more lift in forward flight
options: The opposing airstream is subtracted from its rotational speed
Its pitch angle is increased by the collective
The opposing airstream is added to its rotational speed
cards.explain: The airstream adds to its speed, giving more lift.

cards.question: Why does the retreating blade produce less lift in forward flight
options: The opposing airstream is subtracted from its rotational speed
The opposing airstream is added to its rotational speed
Its pitch angle is reduced by the tail rotor pedals
cards.explain: The airstream subtracts from its speed, giving less lift.

cards.question: How does the speed change along the blade from root to tip
options: It is the same along the span
It decreases towards the blade tip
It increases towards the blade tip
cards.explain: Speed increases toward the tip.

cards.question: In the manual example the helicopter flies forward at 100 kts. How does the relative wind change on the advancing and retreating blades?
options: Advancing +100 kts, retreating -100 kts
Advancing +200 kts, retreating unchanged
Advancing -100 kts, retreating +100 kts
cards.explain: Flight speed adds on the advancing side and subtracts on the retreating side.

cards.question: In the figure 'Dissymmetry of Lift' in forward flight, on which side of the helicopter is the advancing half?
options: The left side
The right side
The rear half
cards.explain: The figure labels the right side as the advancing half.

cards.question: A mass point on a rotating disk is moved towards the edge of the disk. What happens to the rotational speed and why?
options: It stays constant, because the rotor RPM is fixed by the engine
It accelerates, because the mass tries to hold its higher speed
It decelerates, because the mass resists the tangential acceleration
cards.explain: Moving outward needs higher circumferential speed; inertia resists and slows the rotation.

cards.question: A mass point on a rotating disk is moved towards the centre of rotation. What does it do to the rotational speed?
options: It has no effect on the rotational speed
It tries to decelerate the rotational speed
It tries to accelerate the rotational speed
cards.explain: Moving inward, it keeps its higher speed and so accelerates the rotation.

cards.question: Where does the blade's centre of gravity move when the blade flaps upwards
options: Closer towards the blade tip
Closer towards the rotational axis
Closer towards the trailing edge
cards.explain: Upward flapping brings the CG closer to the axis.

cards.question: Where does the blade's centre of gravity move when the blade flaps downwards
options: Closer to the rotational axis
Closer to the blade tip
Closer to the leading edge
cards.explain: Downward flapping moves the CG outward toward the tip.

cards.question: With constant rotor RPM, what does an upward flapping blade do
options: It decelerates and moves backward
It accelerates and moves backward
It accelerates and moves forward
cards.explain: Its CG moves inward, so it speeds up and leads.

cards.question: With constant rotor RPM, what does a downward flapping blade do
options: It decelerates and moves backward
It decelerates and moves forward
It accelerates and moves forward
cards.explain: Its CG moves outward, so it slows down and lags.

cards.question: Why is the installation of a lead-lag hinge required
options: Flapping blades change their pitch angle during each revolution
Flapping blades accelerate or decelerate and move forward or backward
Flapping blades change the direction of the torque reaction
cards.explain: The forward and backward blade movement caused by flapping must be allowed by a lead-lag hinge.

cards.question: In forward flight the advancing blade flaps up. Combining the flapping and centre-of-mass facts, how does this blade move in the plane of rotation?
options: It decelerates and moves backward (lags)
It keeps its position in the plane
It accelerates and moves forward (leads)
cards.explain: The advancing blade flaps up, its CG moves inward, so it accelerates and moves forward.

cards.question: In forward flight the retreating blade flaps down. Combining the flapping and centre-of-mass facts, how does this blade move in the plane of rotation?
options: It accelerates and moves forward (leads)
It keeps its position in the plane
It decelerates and moves backward (lags)
cards.explain: The retreating blade flaps down, its CG moves outward, so it decelerates and lags.

cards.question: Which self-correcting effect comes along with the dissymmetry of lift
options: The lead-lag movement of the blades
The flapping of the blades
The torque of the fuselage
cards.explain: Blade flapping is the self-correcting effect.

cards.question: Why does the advancing blade flap up
options: It experiences decreased relative wind and generates less lift
Its centre of gravity moves closer to the blade tip
It experiences increased relative wind and generates more lift
cards.explain: More relative wind means more lift, so it flaps up.

cards.question: What happens to the angle of attack as the advancing blade flaps up
options: It increases
It stays the same
It decreases
cards.explain: Upward flapping decreases the angle of attack.

cards.question: What happens to the angle of attack as the retreating blade flaps down
options: It increases
It stays the same
It decreases
cards.explain: Downward flapping increases the angle of attack.

cards.question: The retreating blade experiences a decreased relative wind. Which sequence follows according to the manual?
options: Less lift, blade flaps down, angle of attack and lift increase
Less lift, blade flaps up, angle of attack increases
More lift, blade flaps up, angle of attack and lift decrease
cards.explain: The retreating blade flaps down, which raises angle of attack and lift.

cards.question: The advancing blade flaps up in forward flight. What finally happens to its lift?
options: The lift increases as the angle of attack increases
The lift decreases as the angle of attack decreases
The lift stays constant as the pitch is constant
cards.explain: Upward flapping reduces angle of attack and so lift.

cards.question: Is blade flapping alone sufficient to restore rotor balance
options: No, it increases the dissymmetry of lift
No, it helps to balance but is not sufficient
Yes, it fully restores rotor balance
cards.explain: Flapping helps but does not fully restore balance.

cards.question: Why does upward flapping reduce the angle of attack of the advancing blade, using the relative wind rule?
options: Moving up adds a downward relative wind component
Moving up reduces the blade pitch angle
Moving up adds an upward relative wind component
cards.explain: Relative wind is opposite to blade motion, so an upward-moving blade meets air from above, reducing the angle of attack.

cards.question: In the figure 'Blade Flapping', what does upward flapping do to the relative wind and angle of attack?
options: Changes the relative wind and decreases the angle of attack
Changes the relative wind and increases the angle of attack
Leaves the relative wind unchanged and decreases the angle
cards.explain: The figure states upward flapping changes the relative wind and decreases the angle of attack.

cards.question: In the figure 'Blade Flapping', a blade flaps downward. From which direction does the relative wind now meet the blade, and what is the result?
options: From above; the angle of attack increases
From below; the angle of attack decreases
From below; the angle of attack increases
cards.explain: A blade moving down gets relative wind from below, which increases the angle of attack.

cards.question: Why must a rotor blade be able to move and occupy a new position
options: Because the torque reaction turns the fuselage
Because the swash plate rotates with the rotor
Because aerodynamic forces act on the rotor blade
cards.explain: Aerodynamic forces require the blade to move.

cards.question: Which two ways are given to achieve the flexibility for blade flapping
options: A lead-lag hinge or a larger and stiffer tail rotor
A flapping hinge or blade properties that absorb the forces
A feathering hinge or a stronger swash plate bearing
cards.explain: Either a flapping hinge or blades that absorb the forces.

cards.question: Blade flapping compensates dissymmetry of lift. Which hinge lets the blade move up and down for this?
options: Lead-lag hinge
Feathering hinge
Flapping hinge
cards.explain: Flapping hinges allow the up-down movement.

cards.question: When are lead-lag movements always generated
options: When the rotor hovers in ground effect
When a rotor blade is flapping
When the rotor RPM is held constant
cards.explain: Flapping always generates lead-lag movement.

cards.question: Which two causes of blade flapping lead to lead-lag movements
options: Torque reaction or tail rotor pedal inputs
Dissymmetry of lift or cyclic control inputs
Ground effect or collective control inputs
cards.explain: The manual names dissymmetry of lift and cyclic inputs.

cards.question: A pilot makes a cyclic control input. Which chain of effects follows according to the manual?
options: The tail rotor thrust changes, which generates torque
The rotor plane tilts, which generates a lead-lag movement
The swash plate lifts, which generates ground effect
cards.explain: Cyclic tilts the plane, and that generates lead-lag.

cards.question: Which turning force does a counterclockwise turning main rotor generate on the fuselage
options: A counterclockwise turning force
A clockwise turning force
A nose-down pitching force
cards.explain: The fuselage force is opposite, so clockwise.

cards.question: During hover flight, which two jobs does the tail rotor thrust perform
options: Compensate main rotor torque and maintain heading control
Maintain heading control and tilt the rotor disk
Generate lift and compensate main rotor torque
cards.explain: Tail rotor thrust compensates torque and maintains heading.

cards.question: What is translating tendency
options: The drift caused by the thrust of the tail rotor
The turning of the fuselage opposite to the rotor
The drift caused by the ground effect air cushion
cards.explain: Translating tendency is the tail-rotor-thrust drift.

cards.question: How may the pilot prevent the lateral drift due to translating tendency
options: Reduce the tail rotor thrust until the drift stops
Tilt the main rotor disk slightly opposite to the drift
Tilt the main rotor disk slightly in the drift direction
cards.explain: The disk is tilted slightly opposite to the drift.

cards.question: A helicopter in hover drifts sideways although torque is compensated. What causes this drift?
options: The thrust of the tail rotor
Gyroscopic precession
Dissymmetry of lift
cards.explain: The tail rotor's sideways thrust causes translating tendency.

cards.question: During hover, tail rotor thrust makes the helicopter drift to the right. How must the main rotor disk be tilted to prevent this?
options: Slightly to the left
Slightly to the right
Slightly forward
cards.explain: The disk is tilted opposite to the drift, so to the left for a right drift.

cards.question: Which rotor thrust both compensates torque and causes translating tendency
options: The total rotor thrust
The tail rotor thrust
The main rotor thrust
cards.explain: The same tail rotor thrust compensates torque and causes the drift.

cards.question: What is ground effect
options: A condition of reduced performance when hovering near the ground
A condition of improved performance when hovering near the ground
A condition of improved performance in high-speed flight
cards.explain: Ground effect improves performance near the ground.

cards.question: What causes ground effect
options: Increased air density close to the ground surface
Interference of the tail rotor with the main rotor airflow
Interference of the surface with the rotor airflow pattern
cards.explain: The ground surface interferes with the rotor airflow.

cards.question: How does ground effect change as the helicopter gets closer to the ground
options: It remains constant
It becomes more pronounced
It becomes less pronounced
cards.explain: It is more pronounced nearer the ground.

cards.question: Within which height is a helicopter operating in ground effect
options: Within half a rotor diameter
Within two rotor diameters
Within one rotor diameter
cards.explain: In-ground effect is within one rotor diameter.

cards.question: How does the power required to hover in ground effect compare with hovering out of ground effect?
options: More power is required in ground effect
The same power is required in both
Less power is required in ground effect
cards.explain: Hovering in ground effect needs less power.

cards.question: A helicopter hovering out of ground effect descends into an in-ground effect hover. What happens to blade efficiency and why?
options: It increases, because the reduced downward airflow increases the angle of attack
It decreases, because the increased downward airflow reduces the angle of attack
It increases, because the pilot must increase the pitch angle of the blades
cards.explain: Reduced downwash raises angle of attack and efficiency.

cards.question: In ground effect, what happens to the lift vector
options: It tilts toward the tail
It becomes more horizontal
It becomes more vertical
cards.explain: The manual says the lift vector becomes more vertical.

cards.question: In ground effect, what happens to the downward airflow velocity
options: It is reduced
It is unchanged
It is increased
cards.explain: Downwash velocity is reduced.

cards.question: A pilot descends from an out-of-ground effect hover into ground effect and wants to remain in the ground effect hover. What must he do and why?
options: Reduce the blade pitch angle, because rotor efficiency increases
Increase the blade pitch angle, because rotor efficiency decreases
Keep the blade pitch angle, because efficiency is unchanged
cards.explain: Entering ground effect raises angle of attack and efficiency, so pitch is reduced to stay in the hover.

cards.question: A helicopter hovers in ground effect and the pilot climbs out of ground effect without changing the collective. Based on the text, what happens to the power requirement to keep hovering?
options: It increases
It stays the same
It decreases
cards.explain: Hovering out of ground effect needs higher power than in ground effect.

cards.question: During powered flight, how is the rotor drag overcome
options: With rotor inertia
With engine power
With upward airflow
cards.explain: In powered flight, engine power overcomes rotor drag.

cards.question: In which two failure cases must some other force sustain the rotor RPM
options: Tail rotor failure or broken pedals
Engine failure or broken drive shafts
Swash plate failure or broken control rods
cards.explain: Engine failure or broken drive shafts require another force.

cards.question: In which direction does the airflow pass through the main rotor during an autorotative descent
options: From top to bottom
From front to rear
From bottom to top
cards.explain: In autorotation air flows up through the rotor.

cards.question: What provides the energy to overcome blade drag and turn the rotor during autorotation
options: The engine power through the drive shafts
The tail rotor thrust through the gearbox
The airflow passing up through the rotor during descent
cards.explain: Upward airflow during descent drives the rotor.

cards.question: How is the rotor driving force controlled in autorotation
options: By adjusting the collective pitch
By adjusting the engine power lever
By adjusting the tail rotor pedals
cards.explain: The collective pitch controls it.

cards.question: What is the 1st phase of autorotation
options: The controlled descent with the rotor driven by the airflow
The cushioned touchdown using the rotor's kinetic energy
The restart of the engine after the rotor RPM has decayed
cards.explain: The 1st phase is the controlled autorotative descent.

cards.question: What does the pilot do in the 2nd phase of autorotation
options: Uses the tail rotor thrust to slow down the descent
Uses the rotor kinetic energy to cushion the touchdown
Uses the engine power to stop the rate of descent
cards.explain: In the 2nd phase the stored kinetic energy cushions the touchdown.

cards.question: In a controlled autorotative descent, which energy is converted to turn the rotor
options: Electrical energy from the battery
Potential energy due to altitude
Chemical energy from the fuel
cards.explain: Potential energy from altitude drives the rotor.

cards.question: As altitude decreases in autorotation, what happens to the energy stored in the turning rotor?
options: More kinetic energy is converted into potential energy of the helicopter
The stored rotor energy is lost to drag and the rotor comes to a stop
More potential energy is converted into kinetic energy stored in the rotor
cards.explain: Descent converts potential into kinetic energy stored in the rotor.

cards.question: Why must the rotor RPM be sustained after an engine failure
options: So that the engine can be restarted during the descent
So that the tail rotor can be stopped during the descent
So that a controlled flight can be continued to the ground
cards.explain: Rotor RPM keeps the helicopter controllable to the ground.

cards.question: An engine fails in cruise. In which order does the pilot use energy during the autorotation?
options: Engine power drives the rotor in the descent, then altitude cushions touchdown
Altitude drives the rotor in the descent, then rotor kinetic energy cushions touchdown
Rotor kinetic energy cushions the descent, then altitude drives the rotor at touchdown
cards.explain: Phase 1 converts altitude into rotor energy; phase 2 uses the rotor energy for touchdown.
